items.title: One Unit, Counted Up. Alaska's Data Center Scale Ladder
items.summary: A box of about 100 kW is the unit, stacked to every size on record, with maps of District 9 and the Slope lease.
items.content_html:
House District 9 runs from South Anchorage to Whittier. Its data center debate reaches a proposed lease 26 miles south of Deadhorse.

50 to 100 MW, or 3 gigawatts.

One South Anchorage seat.

Stack Holland's top size 30 times. That's 3 GW.

Rep. Ky Holland, an independent who co-chairs House Energy, wants data centers of 50 to 100 MW. Republican John Boyle, a former DNR commissioner, is chief strategy officer at STAK Energy, whose North Slope project ADN describes as 3 gigawatts.

Start with one box. About 100 kilowatts.

UAF's AURORA-AI project with Cordova Electric Cooperative uses modular data centers of about 100 kilowatts each, "about the size of" two large refrigerators, UAF professor Richard Wies told Alaska's News Source. Every block in this deck is built from it.

Alaska has drawn lines at 5 MW and 15 MW.

Fairbanks Borough Mayor Grier Hopkins proposes pausing permits for data centers of 5 MW or more until December 31st, 2027. SB 250 would have exempted those under 15 MW. It passed the Senate 14 to 5 on May 16th, then was held in a House committee.

From South Anchorage to Whittier, one seat.

House District 9 spans South Anchorage, the Lower Hillside, Girdwood and Whittier. Nearly 44 percent of its registered voters cast an August primary ballot, 16 points above the state average, ADN reported.

Holland's line sits at 50 to 100 MW.

Holland, who worked on building data centers in the Lower 48, calls hyperscale in Alaska "a fantasy idea." He wants "purpose-built, strategic, modest-sized" facilities and cites limited bandwidth, distance from markets and infrastructure challenges.

STAK's lease ground, 26 miles south of Deadhorse.

Boyle, STAK Energy's chief strategy officer, is open to large North Slope data centers, where gas could ease power generation. He says they must avoid "the negative externalities that we see in the Lower 48."

3 GW tops Alaska's net summer capacity.

EIA counted 2,853 MW of net summer generating capacity statewide in 2024. ADN describes STAK's project as 3 gigawatts.

Every size on the record, on one ladder.

Where should Alaska's line sit, in megawatts?

SB 250's sponsor returns next year. District 9 votes November 3rd.

items.title: One Line of Code in a Polar Bear Rule
items.summary: Both versions of the line, the dens it skipped, the infrared survey and the March and October numbers.
items.content_html:
6 to 22. Fixing one line of code moved a Fish and Wildlife Service estimate of harassed denning polar bears that far.

One line of code. Harassed denning bears went 6 to 22.

It counted only the dens marked undisturbed.

A den with a missing value matched neither, so the old line skipped it. The new one counts it.

Quiet all winter. Disturbed after emergence.

The faulty output gave them 0 percent take. Fixed, each carries a 28 percent chance of Level B harassment for the sow and 72 percent of Level A for the cubs.

FWS's den take figures come from a simulation run 10,000 times.

About 6.5 dens a year sit within a mile of the work, the same in March and October.

To the eye, a den is one more drift.

From the air, the survey looks for heat.

Cameras on fixed-wing aircraft read a denning female's body heat through the snow, four times likelier to find a den than infrared from the ground, FWS says.

What the fixes changed, and what they didn't.

Vessel takes fell 16 to 10 in a separate fix to routes counted twice. Industry's own estimate is 123 bears, Level B only.

Fixed, then weighed no higher than industry's estimate.

FWS concedes the model's figures significantly exceed historical data and AOGA's. AOGA and one other commenter call it seriously flawed and not validated. FWS says the code and inputs are public.

FWS says the code is public. Should the model count for more?

The first den survey window opens November 25th.

items.title: AIDEA's Fiber Tool and NuCube Stake, Cut Open
items.summary: Eight conditions drawn as cable armor, four subsea cables by age, a NuCube price ladder and both checks side by side.
items.content_html:
AIDEA called two very different things an "investment" on October 21st.

$75 million behind eight locks. $25 million at $9.25 a share.

Eight conditions wrap any deal.

Up to $75 million, all-in, cost overruns and capital calls included. Memoranda and forecasts don't count as customers.

At the core, glass that has to come ashore.

Every investment must deliver fiber pairs or capacity that physically land in Alaska and can be used there. A binding deal must also set a minimum number of landing pairs, with defined capacity and access rights.

Alaska has four subsea cables to the Lower 48. Two date from 1999.

The resolution puts a subsea system's typical design life at about 25 years. None of the systems landing in Alaska connects directly to Asia.

"The routes chosen in the next few years will last for decades."

Same day, $25 million for a reactor company.

AIDEA announced a $25 million equity investment in NuCube Energy. Its NuSun platform is built around a solid-state, heat-pipe-cooled microreactor. AIDEA's release names no Alaska site, utility, customer or deployment date.

The $25 million buys shares, not a reactor.

Class A shares at $9.25, about 14.5 percent under the $10.82 reference price. It counts toward NuCube's $75 million minimum cash to close its merger. NuCube's filing cites AI data center energy demand. The fiber resolution never does.

The two checks, side by side.

Should AIDEA's next equity check carry locks like the fiber money?

items.title: What's Dated in the Houston Land Transfer and What Isn't
items.summary: Inside are Crowther's words, the complaint and its summons, the four steps to a deed and a ledger of what's dated and what isn't.
items.content_html:
Alaska's Houston land transfer has a date for the lawsuit and the inauguration but not for the day 19,950 acres change hands.

The decision could beat December 7th. The handoff likely won't.

"Certainly possible."

He told senators "using our land for development has been the governor's priority." Surveying, the appeal period and the lawsuit would likely carry the transfer past December 7th, ADN reported.

A lawsuit cites seven sections of the constitution.

Eric Forrer and David Eastman sued the State, DNR and Governor Dunleavy. AIDEA isn't a named party. "We sued just to stop him," Forrer told the Mat-Su Sentinel.

The State's 40 days start only at service.

DNR hadn't been served when the Mat-Su Sentinel asked.

A decision isn't a deed.

If DNR approves, survey, plat, title and closing must be completed before any conveyance. On October 8th AIDEA's Randy Ruaro told lawmakers no developer, tenant, power source or site plan exists, KTUU reported.

19,950 acres.

More than 2,000 people can ask DNR to reconsider.

Only people who sent timely written comment can appeal DNR's Final Finding and Decision. Comments closed September 14th, and DNR is still reviewing them, ADN reported.

What has a date, and what doesn't.

December 7th ends a term. It doesn't survey 19,950 acres.

Save this for the day DNR's Final Finding lands.

items.title: 96 Trillion Cubic Feet, No Way to Market
items.summary: The USGS count and its 17.3 to 276.7 trillion cubic foot range, reinjected gas, both buyers and the pipe on south-up maps.
items.content_html:
The USGS counts a mean 96 trillion cubic feet of undiscovered North Slope gas. The same fact sheet says it has no route to market at scale.

96 trillion cubic feet. "No method" to market it.

Counted from the mountains to 3 miles offshore.

The USGS mean is 96 trillion cubic feet of gas not yet discovered. The same page says "there is no method for bringing natural gas to markets at large commercial scales."

A risked range, not reserves.

Even the gas already found goes back down.

Most gas that comes up with North Slope oil is pumped back underground to hold reservoir pressure.

The count stops at the mountains. If the gas can't cross them, the buyer comes to the gas.

715.4 acres beside the Dalton, 26 miles south of Deadhorse.

DNR's preliminary decision would lease it to STAK Energy for 50 years, for a gas-powered facility with modular high-performance computing units. A gigawatt or more, per the Anchorage Press. More than 500 comments came in.

Pitched as the world's largest gas power plant.

North Slope Power, from the North Slope Borough and Twenty First Century Utilities, plans 3 gigawatts first and up to 10, for colocated AI data centers.

800 miles of pipe, still no decision.

It would carry North Slope gas to an export terminal on Cook Inlet. Its final investment decision, first proposed for last year, still hasn't been made.

Until a pipe exists, first claim on North Slope gas goes to whoever builds beside it.

Should the Legislature decide who gets it first?

items.title: The Sky Has No State Rule. The Ground Does Now.
items.summary: Inside are the night of the flights, the payload, a radar estimate against a rain gauge, each government's own words and the ten-line form.
items.content_html:
Drones seeded clouds over Kachemak Bay on August 23rd. On October 20th the Kenai Peninsula Borough's pending seeding rule passed 7 to 0.

The sky has no state rule. The ground does now.

Two drones seeded the clouds. The borough answered.

On August 23rd Rainmaker flew two drones it calls autonomous from near the head of Kachemak Bay. On October 20th the borough Assembly voted 7 to 0, two absent, to require a lease or permit for weather modification on borough land.

19 flares. 374 grams of silver iodide.

Each red flare dispersed about 19.7 grams. The new form asks every applicant for each flare's quantity, type, manufacturer, serial number and total weight, plus a safety data sheet for anything released.

Radar saw it. The water was modeled.

Rainmaker's report puts the first radar signature 40.4 minutes after release, during seven seeding missions between 0618 and 0954 UTC. DEC calls the result a modeled estimate, not a measurement of water collected at the ground.

19 million gallons. About 0.01 inches.

Rainmaker puts the added precipitation at 57.62 acre-feet across 249.53 square kilometers, with a range of 41.70 to 89.35. Spread over that area, Rainmaker says, it's about a hundredth of an inch.

0954 UTC. Seeding ends.

Nobody needed a state permit to start.

Whose sky is it?

Reporting, not a comprehensive permitting program, DEC says. No DEC permit required. No framework specific to weather modification. DNR sent a letter of no objection. Can't fully regulate weather modification or airspace, its legal memo says. So it ruled its own land.

Before seeding from borough land, name the outcome. Then list ten things.

Skip the signed closeout and it's $1,000 a day, plus a 5-year ban.

Which should Alaska choose?

The borough asked the Legislature to ban cloud seeding or require a permit.

items.title: Only Two Zones, 97 Percent of the Map
items.summary: The zoning map by acre, the industrial sliver, the floor test drawn to scale and 5 MW against GVEA's alert lines.
items.content_html:
A proposed Fairbanks ordinance says today's code permits a large data center in only two zones. Neither is industrial.

"Only" two zones.

97 percent of the map.

The draft says "only" GU-1 and GU-5. They are nearly all of it.

Under today's code, the ordinance says, a large data center would be permitted only in these two General Use districts.

Everything else fits in 3 percent.

Every district besides GU-1 and GU-5 covers 145,827 acres. Heavy Industrial is 3,555 of them, Light Industrial 5,929. By the draft's own reading of today's code, neither one qualifies.

Written in 2005, before AI demand.

The draft says the code doesn't address data centers as a use. General Use, the widest zone, is where they fall.

The pause makes news. The definition decides.

Under the draft, a data center is large at 5 MW of peak demand, more than 50,000 square feet of data center floor, or 5 MW of onsite generation. Any one test is enough.

If adopted, no applications accepted and none approved through December 31st, 2027.

Is 5 MW large? Ask the reserve.

GVEA's Level 1 alert starts below 38 MW of reserve, Level 2 below 15 MW. Its first alert, October 12th, reached Level 2, with two units in maintenance and a third offline.

The line gets argued now.

The agenda sends the draft to the Planning Commission, recommendation due in 90 days. A commission work session on the final Comprehensive Plan is set for October 27th. If adopted, a study of energy, air, water and noise follows within six months.

Is 5 MW the right line for "large" in Fairbanks?

items.content_html:
"We're going to file to intervene and oppose it, just so we have a position," AEA's chief said of the proposed Cook Inlet AI data center.

Priority to study, not permission to build.

items.title: The State Flew the Kuskokwim. An AI Prospector Arrived.
items.summary: One real McGrath flight line's magnetic profile, a map and a card of five state surveys, the Ganes Creek radiometrics printed with three grant numbers, and an empty pocket for a first Alaska property, none named yet.
items.content_html:
On June 23rd, 2024, four fixed-wing aircraft began flying the Kuskokwim for the state's McGrath survey.

86,319 km of public survey lines. Now an AI prospector.

On October 20th, an AI prospect generator set up in Alaska.

Geomorphic AI formed Golden Dyke Exploration LLC, a wholly owned Alaska subsidiary. Its release says new state airborne surveys extend decades of USGS and state mapping. It names no Alaska property yet.

It packages the target, not the drill.

Geomorphic says its role is to generate and package targets, then advance them through joint ventures and earn-ins while keeping an interest. It doesn't fund or operate drilling. It hasn't said whether it uses these surveys.

Lines 400 meters apart, about 100 meters up.

Four fixed-wing aircraft flew McGrath over two summers, 86,319 line kilometers in all. A cesium sensor read the rock's magnetism. Two gamma-ray spectrometers read its radiation.

The McGrath block, read every 400 meters.

Five surveys, one scale.

Paid for by Earth MRI. Free to download.

Federal Earth MRI grants paid for the flying. The state posts the data under an open end-user license. DGGS says it will promote resource exploration of the central Kuskokwim.

Open input. Private output.

The flying, the grids and the license are public. A packaged target moves through private deals, with an interest kept. Geomorphic has named no Alaska property yet.

Should a target built on public surveys say which ones it used?

items.title: Played Bethel's Yup'ik, the Model Answered Across the Sea
items.summary: Bethel's gold pin threads the slides past 111 pins on St. Lawrence Island, the label lists, KYUK's archive, the pilot, the speakers who label next and resolution 26-20.
items.content_html:
Meta's model card says "This model supports 4017 languages." "Supports" for Yup'ik means one label in 4,017.

Played Bethel's Yup'ik, the model most often answered across the sea.

111 to 110.

Played Yup'ik clips from KYUK's broadcasts, Meta's MMS-LID answered Central Siberian Yupik 111 times and Yup'ik 110. That language is spoken on St. Lawrence Island and in eastern Russia.

Three big open models list no Yupik at all.

Only Meta's largest model lists Yup'ik, one label in 4,017. The authors say a label space that big makes out-of-the-box results poor for languages with little data.

Central Siberian Yupik is a living language. One count puts about 1,000 speakers on St. Lawrence Island. The model's top miss was a near one.

The test audio came from Bethel's own station.

KYUK airs about an hour of local news in Yup'ik a day. The researchers labeled 9 of its videos, 5.1 hours, through the American Archive of Public Broadcasting.

The labeled hours lifted recall to 0.92.

Trained on labeled Yup'ik and Samoan clips, a small classifier on a frozen Whisper encoder lifted Yup'ik recall from 0.41 to 0.92. It chooses among four labels, not 4,017. The authors call it pilot-scale.

The next labels come from speakers.

The pilot's labels were written by in-house researchers, not native speakers. The authors plan to hand that work to trained native-speaker annotators, and community language fellows have begun, the paper says.

AFN is set to take up 26-20.

From the Metlakatla and Ketchikan Indian Communities, it seeks permanent, non-competitive federal language funding for every eligible Tribe. Technology and archives are among its uses. It never mentions AI. Committee and board say do pass.

Whoever labels the hours draws the map.

What does a model builder owe the speakers who write the next labels?

items.title: One Rock, Two Readings of the Kenai Loop Gas Storage Lease
items.summary: Both estimates, each side's evidence, both plans and the pore space claim.
items.content_html:
Under Kenai's airport, ownership changes once, then splits.

One rock. Two readings.

The state backed the one with the data.

Same reservoir. Two estimates of the gas left.

ENSTAR put the gas left at 3.9 Bcf. Hilcorp said 6.4. The state found ENSTAR's figure more reliable and favors ENSTAR's storage lease.

Two sands, sealed in coal.

The gas sits in the pores of these sands. The state and the City of Kenai each claim that pore space.

The state judged what each company showed it.

ENSTAR gave DNR a dynamic reservoir model. DNR says Hilcorp provided about one quarter of the requested data and no model. Hilcorp couldn't comment before Alaska Public Media's story.

Two plans for one field.

ENSTAR says it could fall 18 days short of gas this winter, depending on temperatures.

Cook Inlet peaked at 196 Bcf in 2006. In-state demand is about 70 now.

DNR projects production below demand in the early 2030s. Hilcorp told legislators nearly all of the roughly 30 Bcf it holds in Pool 6 is committed to ENSTAR.

The model reads the rock. It can't read the deed.

DNR asserts the state has clear authority over the pore space. Kenai's city manager wrote that the city owns it, citing Pioneer Law, and warned of "conflicting leases."

Comment to DNR by 5 p.m. November 13th.

The finding is preliminary. The Director decides after reading the comments.

items.title: A Year After Halong, the Map Under the AI Forecast
items.summary: Maps show the grid NOAA's AI model learned from, the Delta's dark stations, Halong's turn east and its saltwater on the tundra.
items.content_html:
NOAA's 16-day AI forecast now finishes in about 40 minutes. Y-K Delta airport stations have gone days or weeks with no observations.

Forecasts now run on AI. The map under them has holes.

An AI forecast starts from a map of measurements.

NOAA fine-tuned its AI model, AIGFS, on its own Global Data Assimilation System analyses. That system puts surface, balloon, aircraft, buoy, radar and satellite observations onto a three-dimensional grid.

Days or weeks with no observations.

Since April, every airport weather station in the Y-K Delta region has gone days or weeks without observations at times, climatologist Rick Thoman told KYUK.

The models had the track. They missed the shift east.

Global models forecast Halong's track into the Bering Sea well but failed to forecast its eastward shift, Thoman said. A lack of balloon launches across Western Alaska may have played a role, KYUK reported.

Saltwater ran more than 15 miles onto the tundra.

More than 1,500 people were forced from their homes. In Kipnuk, 90% of buildings were damaged or destroyed, KYUK reported.

What got faster. What went missing.

"We need ocean observations."

"Speed and skill are not the same as trustworthiness."

AI sea ice forecast systems barely existed a decade ago and now number in the dozens, researchers wrote in Eos on October 9th. The observations needed to build and test them remain sparse across both poles.

Where should Alaska's next observation go?

"I'm not just talking more [FAA] weather stations."

items.title: Houston's 19,950 acres, and the answer owed October 26th
items.summary: First comes DNR's refusal to attend and the subpoena, then the land and its price, the committee's size test, both reverters and the dated record.
items.content_html:
Commissioner Crowther, your department would keep a take-back clause on 885 acres at Port MacKenzie and waive it on 19,950 acres at Houston.

"The Governor's office has not given us permission to attend."

DECLINING AN OCTOBER 8TH HEARING ON 19,950 ACRES

Senators voted to subpoena him.

On October 14th Senate Resources voted to subpoena Natural Resources Commissioner John Crowther. DNR confirmed a day later that he will appear on October 26th at 10 a.m.

About 19,950 acres of state land, at no cost for the land.

About 31 square miles, two miles north of Houston, to the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority under the public and charitable use statute. AIDEA would cover survey and closing costs, not the land's value.

94 percent of other transfers under it were under 100 acres.

This one is about 200 times that. The law sets no size limit, the Legislature's lawyer wrote, and he was not aware of any earlier transfer to AIDEA under it.

"The scope of this decision does not include AIDEA's post-patent use."

The decision lists scalable data centers among AIDEA's possible uses. On October 8th AIDEA's director called a data center there implausible, Alaska's News Source reported.

Port MacKenzie's draft keeps a reverter. Houston's would waive it.

DNR's Port MacKenzie decision includes a five year take-back clause on 885 acres. Without one, the Legislature's lawyer wrote on September 4th, no legal mechanism after patent keeps the land serving a public purpose.

41.8 miles of trail already cross it.

They tie into the Haessler-Norris. The committee lists mushing, four-wheeling and snowmachining.

July 10th to October 26th

Why waive the reverter at Houston and keep it at Port MacKenzie?

What should the first question be?

items.title: One Gigawatt, to Scale
items.summary: Every frame is 100 MW wide at one scale, so the carousel is one gigawatt long. On it are the 15 MW cushion, five data center sizes and a planned 70 MW battery.
items.content_html:
UAF's new guide counts a state transportation container of drone imagery as a data center.

Fairbanks' grid had 15 MW to spare.

This carousel is one gigawatt wide.

Level 2. One backup unit left.

Golden Valley issued its first Energy Emergency Alert after a third unit failed while two were down for planned maintenance. It hasn't said which one. Its alert page puts Level 2 at reserves below 15 MW.

"Probably not going to be a one-off."

It says it has met Level 1 and Level 2 conditions on numerous occasions over the past year. It lost access to power from Anchorage-area gas plants as Cook Inlet gas ran short.

"Want to drop 10 billion on a data center"

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said it in Fairbanks two days after the alert, and named no investor. Alaska has seen proposals for as many as 15 data centers, Alaska Public Media reports. A dollar figure and a count. Neither is a megawatt.

The guide's two smallest sizes fall under 15 MW.

UAF's energy center sizes an edge site at about 0.1 to 0.5 MW, like the state transportation department's drone imagery container. Enterprise runs about 0.5 to 10 MW, like the University of Alaska's and Providence's.

Five sizes, one ruler.

No hyperscale site runs in Alaska.

The guide cites one proposal, STAK on the North Slope. No large cloud provider runs a region here. On the Railbelt, it says, the biggest sizes may need significant new generation and transmission.

The fixes take years.

A planned battery would deliver 70 MW for up to 2 hours, at about $130 million. A used LM6000 turbine, or an equivalent, is under evaluation at up to $80 million. Construction of the Beluga to Healy line isn't expected until after 2030.

"How much change is our community prepared to absorb?"

That was one gigawatt.

What size of data center, if any, should Fairbanks say yes to?

items.title: Software Can Read the Tape. The Camera Is the Cost.
items.summary: From the camera on its mast to the same camera on a hatch, the deck shows 76 of 172 boats that would move, a 3-trip tally, cheaper trips, 96 of 97 sharks, a $6,003 gear case, the Gulf's 14.25 percent and an empty berth.
items.content_html:
"Should not have to carry one less crew member," the North Pacific Council's Advisory Panel said of boats sent from cameras to observers.

Software can read the tape. 76 boats would still lose the camera.

172 camera boats. 76 would move.

39 took no trips in three years. 37 more averaged under 3 trips a year. The other boats stay on camera.

Under 3 trips a year, the camera goes to a boat that fishes.

NMFS's draft starts the yearly check with the 2028 plan, at least 9 trips over 3 years. In 2027, 32 boats that filed no monitoring plan since 2024 go to observers first.

Monitored trips get cheaper.

About $96,000 shifts to boats that fish.

96 of 97

Pacific sleeper sharks, found on longline camera video by a machine-learning model.

Reading the tape is the cheap part.

NMFS calls the camera gear a high buy-in, about $6,003 a boat a year, while reviewing a selected trip adds little. It intends to support scaling the AI tools in 2027, if staff are available.

The Gulf's fixed-gear catch is the least watched.

NMFS expects 1,010 Gulf fixed-gear camera trips in 2027, against 92 in the Bering Sea, and plans to review 154 of the Gulf's.

A camera takes no bunk. An observer does.

The panel said a boat moved to observers shouldn't have to leave a crew member ashore. The Council asked NMFS to consider active boats that can prove they have no bunk for one.

3 trips a year to keep a camera. Fair line, or wrong test?

Final rates are expected in December.

items.title: 112 Answers in Palmer, and Where They Go
items.summary: Pictured are the room's phones, the Houston land, the Port MacKenzie parcels, a gavel on SB 250 and the voting calendar.
items.content_html:
22 legislative candidates were in a Palmer theater on October 4th as the crowd answered a question on AI data centers.

57 of 112 said outlaw large AI data centers in Mat-Su.

Three other rooms decide.

57 outlaw. 47 regulate. 8 allow.

The Mat-Su Sentinel asked it live. The tally built on screen as phones answered.

A room, not a poll of Mat-Su.

About 200 came. 112 answered, and each could see the tally grow. 22 legislative candidates were there too.

The question said "the state." Here, that's three rooms.

DNR holds land near Houston. The University of Alaska leased land at Port MacKenzie. A data center bill stopped in the Legislature.

About 19,950 acres. Comments closed September 14th.

A preliminary decision would convey it to AIDEA, whose plan lists data centers among possible uses. AIDEA says none is proposed. As of late September, there is no final decision.

829 acres. Leased in late May, for 20 years.

To Terra Energy, according to university officials.

A data center bill passed the Senate, then stopped.

SB 250 passed the Senate 14 to 5 on May 16th. A House committee heard and held it on May 18th, and it didn't pass the House before the session ended.

22 candidates for those seats were in the room.

The format didn't ask them to debate. Early voting opens October 19th. Election Day is November 3rd.

Ask your House and Senate candidates before October 19th.

items.title: Who Sets the Clock on a Plate Read
items.summary: The three texts' clocks, the September definition built on AI, APD's 14-day policy and the store readers none reach.
items.content_html:
In the Anchorage mayor's version of the surveillance ordinance, a plate data "limit" is a reason, not a number.

14 days in code, or a limit set in policy?

Three texts. One sets a day.

The sponsors' August 18th original would delete plate data within 14 days, and searching older data would need a warrant. The mayor's September 15th substitute asks for a policy limit "based on articulable operational needs." The sponsors' own S-1 builds on the mayor's text.

The original timed the live feed too.

Live camera access would shut off after sixty minutes, renewed thirty at a time. Trials of new tools, 90 days at most. Plate reader authority, ending January 1st, 2031. The September texts set other clocks, 30 days to report a policy change and 45 to act on a complaint.

September's texts name artificial intelligence.

Both define surveillance technology as tools that work "by using fully or partially-automated machine learning, artificial intelligence, or similar technology." The August original defined it by what a system collects.

There is already a 14.

APD's own page says scanned plate data is deleted after 14 days. That's police policy on a web page, not code.

Three texts, side by side.

No version reaches this pole.

Flock says it began installing plate readers for a private customer in Alaska the week before October 5th. A crowdsourced map showed eight at two Anchorage Lowe's stores, ADN reports. APD says it doesn't use Flock and has no access to them. Each text governs city agencies.

October 20th could set the city's clock.

The Assembly returns to AO 2026-108 on October 20th, after a work session scheduled for October 14th. The crime center it governs could connect up to 750 cameras. In late August, 238 were registered with APD and 11 integrated, per KTUU.

Where should Anchorage write its number, in code or in policy?

Say which below.

items.title: Fairbanks So Far. A 123-Vote Lead, 1,235 Ballots Out
items.summary: Election Day is set against early voting, then 32 precincts, Eielson's 24 Election Day ballots and every unofficial total.
items.content_html:
The unofficial Fairbanks results printed at 9:57 a.m. on October 7th carry two columns of zeros, absentee and questioned.

A 123-vote lead. 1,235 ballots still out.

Ramirez won Election Day. Early voting carried Howell.

Howell agreed with the idea of a data center moratorium. Election Day ballots went to Ramirez 6,251 to 5,612. Early ballots went to Howell 1,618 to 856. Seat H ran the same way, Leaders ahead on Election Day and Crass ahead early.

Ramirez carried 20 precincts. Howell carried 12.

Ramirez's widest was Chena Lakes, 359 to 123. Howell's was Goldstream #2, 323 to 117. The 2,603 early ballots aren't split by precinct. They sit in one row of the clerk's report.

27 of 32 precincts went the same way in every seat.

In 11, Election Day chose Howell, LaJiness and Crass. In 16, it chose Ramirez, Shupe and Leaders.

15,141 of 77,227 registered voters, counted so far.

24 Election Day ballots from 2,103 registered voters.

The Pentagon wants up to a dozen military data centers near Anchorage, Healy and Fairbanks. The moratorium the Assembly asked for names state-owned or municipal land. Fort Wainwright's precinct cast 59 of 3,256 on Election Day.

The count so far

The qualified rest is counted on October 13th.

811 absentee and 424 questioned ballots. Only qualified ballots count, and not every one marks Seat D. Certification is scheduled for October 22nd.

items.title: Alaska's Newest Rare-Earth AI Won't Hunt for Ore
items.summary: Pictured are a grain of coal ash, Healy coal from earlier UAA lab work, the one named microbe, both AI jobs and who holds the money.
items.content_html:
Brandon Briggs's UAA team holds $3,824,575 of a $6 million NSF bet on microbes and AI for rare earths in coal refuse and ash.

Alaska's newest rare-earth AI won't hunt for ore. It will mind microbes.

Two jobs, and neither is prospecting.

A $6 million NSF project led by UAA plans to pull rare earths out of coal refuse and ash with microbes. AI is to rank the waste first, then run the tank as power comes and goes.

Alaska doesn't mine rare earths. Coal holds a little.

Researcher D'Lynn Gleason said so in earlier UAA lab work on coal donated by Usibelli Coal Mine in Healy. She said that coal carries rare earths, scandium and yttrium among them, too thin to mine with acid.

One microbe is named.

The award names Shewanella oneidensis. It will be tested on cost and life-cycle metrics.

Rank the waste before it's fed.

UAF says AI will help predict how readily rare earths can be recovered from different materials. The award calls it a Virtual Assay to screen feedstocks. It is planned, not built.

The power dips. Something has to decide what the tank does.

Job two, the Alaska part.

Reinforcement-learning controllers will learn inside a digital twin of the bioreactor, linked to microgrid simulators, and adjust it as energy availability changes. The award's own word is energy-constrained.

About $6 million, to August 31st, 2030.

Began September 1st. One of eight EPSCoR projects sharing $39.9 million.

New deposits, or old waste? Where should Alaska point its mineral AI?

items.title: 829 Acres, 20 Years, and a Notice That Named No Tenant
items.summary: Four parcels to scale and the notice's dates, the rent by year, the affiliate's coal plan and the 6-1 vote.
items.content_html:
On January 30th the University of Alaska put 829 acres at Port MacKenzie up for lease on a notice that named no tenant.

829 acres. 20 years.

The notice named no tenant.

Terra Energy is the tenant.

Signed in late May for 20 years. The lease describes the Terra Energy Center Campus as "a large-scale industrial park," with energy generation, transmission, storage and distribution among its uses, and lets Terra sublease to future tenants.

An inholding in the borough's port.

The four parcels sit inside the Mat-Su Borough's 8,000-acre port district. Borough officials weren't told before the university signed. Port manager Dave Griffin said it "blows my mind."

Comment was asked on a notice that named no lessee and no use.

Posted January 30th. Comments closed at 5 p.m. on March 2nd. The lease was signed in late May, per university officials.

University land skips the best interest finding.

Projects on university land are exempt from the finding the state requires for major actions on state land, per the Mat-Su Sentinel.

$20,000 the first year. $586,000 once it operates.

Then $60,000 a year in years two and three. Construction would begin in 2029, and the report gives no figure for that year. Operations are targeted for 2030, and rent would rise 2 percent a year to the end of the 20-year lease.

The campus is part of a coal plan.

Flatlands Energy plans a coal plant near Skwentna. DOE selected the project for $89 million in engineering funding for a planned 1,250 MW plant and lists data centers among the loads it would serve. The university's own information doesn't highlight data centers.

The borough markets land with Terra.

In March the Assembly overrode a veto 6-1 to court large power users with Terra, data centers among them. Officials expect Terra to seek about 1,000 borough acres near the port.

Should a university land notice name its purpose before comments close?

items.title: Alaska's Second Wire Has a Passenger List
items.summary: Today's intertie, the new wire's stops and money, three bases and Murkowski's sentence, then five records, two saying data center.
items.content_html:
Alaska's planned second power line would end at Healy, south of Clear and Eielson, where the Air Force offered land for AI data centers.

Alaska's second wire has a passenger list.

Data centers aren't on it.

The money names the military, and mining.

Energy Secretary Chris Wright tied the project to "the major U.S. military expansion currently underway in Alaska" and to mining. DOE says the line adds a pathway to "major military installations." The release never says data center.

One line joins the two halves today.

AEA's Alaska Intertie runs 170 miles from Willow to Healy. The state built it in the mid-1980s.

The record names its stops and its price. Not its route.

The Alaska delegation lists the Beluga substation, West Susitna, Willow and Healy. AEA's Curtis Thayer told the Alaska Beacon the federal money will likely go to engineering, planning and permitting.

On Railbelt bases, land offered for AI data centers.

Proposals were due June 29th. None had been awarded as of late September, per the American Homefront Project. Most of Alaska's bases use power that flows through the intertie, the Alaska Beacon reports.

One corridor. No second path between the halves.

"I am not a proponent of data centers down at JBER or at our interior installations because we are not able to support them because of an insecure energy base at this time."

Five records. Two say "data center." The one with the money doesn't.

Reading them side by side is this deck's work, not DOE's.

Should the Beluga to Healy line be planned with data center load in it, or without?

1.1 percent.

items.title: More Than Three Alaskas of Power, Planned for Prudhoe Bay
items.summary: What EIA measures is drawn sharp, all 152 plants mapped to scale. The reported money sits in fog. The terms are a closed pipe blind.
items.content_html:
3,000 megawatts. Phase one of a gas plant planned near Prudhoe Bay for AI data centers nearly equals all 152 power plants in Alaska.

More than three Alaskas of power, planned for Prudhoe Bay.

Each lit bore is 100 MW.

Phase one is about the size of every power plant in Alaska combined. The full plan is more than three times it.

A borough's plant, for AI data centers.

The North Slope Borough and Twenty First Century Utilities (TFC) are developing North Slope Power to feed colocated AI data centers. The borough's own utility runs seven village plants, 21.4 MW in all.

The gas is already here.

Two outlets, two areas, two counts. Gas is already Alaska's main fuel for electricity, per EIA. In March the borough's mayor and TFC took the plan to CERAWeek in Texas.

TFC's proposal listed climate change among 10 North Slope challenges. Where it said how it would tackle each one, climate change got "N/A."

$6.2 million in.

A $1.2 million no-bid feasibility contract in November 2025. Another $5 million of public funds in March. Both as reported by the Alaska Current.

The terms aren't public.

That is the resolution behind the $5 million, as the Alaska Current quotes it. It says the Borough would "initially" keep that majority. The financial structure is not public.

items.title: Ten Minutes of Every Hour, The Count an AI Drone Must Beat
items.summary: The Togiak's 119,298 sockeye are traced from a ten-minute window to their own error bar.
items.content_html:
"The results have exceeded my expectations," Norm Van Vactor said in July of his Wood River AI drone pilot.

Togiak missed by 702 fish. Its tower counted 10 minutes an hour.

Ten minutes, times six.

Bristol Bay's towers count each bank for 10 minutes of every hour, then expand. Crews work around the clock with hand clickers. At six to one, the Togiak's 119,298 rests on roughly 19,883 fish someone saw.

The error bar runs three times the miss.

ADF&G put the average sampling CV across nine Bristol Bay tower projects at 0.02 in 2004 and 2005. On the Togiak's 119,298 that is about 2,400 fish either way. It assumes no miscounts inside the ten minutes.

The rule was tested on 12 to 80 hours.

In 1965 and 1966, crews counted whole hours and compared them with the first 10 minutes, expanded. Errors ran generally under 10 percent, with no significant bias.

Eight towers counted 12.3 million of 15.6 million.

A box opens. A drone takes off.

A computer vision model is learning to pick out the salmon in its footage.

A key press for every fish.

Technicians press a key each time a fish crosses a line drawn on the footage. The first phase logged 256 flights and 17,552 images, stitched into 117 orthomosaics. The project lead says it spots fish 12 to 18 hours before the tower.

Matching the tower can't be the bar.

The pilot plans to test its model against Fish and Game tower counts next. Tower sampling error averaged about 2 percent in 2004 and 2005. The team's goal is a count with a stated confidence. Write the margin first.

Before the Wood River test runs, who should set the passing margin?

items.title: Alaska's SNAP Bill Reads a Year That Opened Thursday
items.summary: Steel instruments read the law's shares and Alaska's record, then the state's system, staffing and 2028 fix.
items.content_html:
Alaska's SNAP payment error rate ran 57, 60.4, 24.7 and 23 percent from 2022 to 2025.

Alaska's SNAP bill reads a year that opened Thursday.

Fiscal 2027 is read either way.

From fiscal 2029, a state's share uses its error rate from three fiscal years before. Fiscal 2030 reads fiscal 2027, opened October 1st, whichever start applies.

The first share moved on Thursday.

Washington's share of SNAP administration fell from 50 to 25 percent, so Alaska now pays 75. Legislative Finance estimates about $6.6 million more a year. The Anchorage Daily News reported nearly $11 million.

The second share is a staircase.

Under 6 percent, a state pays none of the benefit cost. At 10 or more, it pays 15 percent.

The record, against the statute's lines.

Alaska's 2025 rate, times 1.5, cleared 20 percent, which moved its start to fiscal 2029. Clear it again in 2026 and the start moves to 2030.

"COBOL on a mainframe."

How the state describes EIS, its legacy eligibility system. ARIES, the newer one, holds only MAGI Medicaid.

218 of 332 positions filled.

The yearly average left 34.3 percent vacant. "During periods when Alaska had significant workload backlogs, that had a larger impact on the state's error rate," the Department of Health wrote.

The fix is scheduled for 2028.

Milestone 2, estimated at $20 million, began in October 2025. Milestone 2.5, estimated at $5 million, would move SNAP data off the mainframe. The Department says the biggest gains wait for full modernization.

Save this for the day fiscal 2026's rate is published.

items.title: Three Yeas, Three Short, No Start Date
items.summary: Gold marks Alaska's three yeas in a 100-cup Senate tray at 57 and a 432-cup House tray at 417, beside two unturned sand-glasses, a three-bay exemption cabinet, SB 250's 14 and 5 and a steel rule with no enactment tick.
items.content_html:
On the Alaska Senate floor in Juneau on May 16th, data center bill SB 250 passed 14 to 5.

Alaska's three votes were yes. The Senate fell three short.

Cloture needed 60. It got 57.

Three-fifths of the Senate had to agree just to take it up. The motion was then withdrawn. Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan both voted yea. The House had passed it two weeks before.

Two weeks earlier, the House passed it 417 to 3.

Nick Begich voted yea. Republicans went 210 to 0, Democrats 206 to 3 and the one independent voted yea. Suspending the rules took two-thirds.

A standard for computing sites of 100 MW and up.

Rates would be designed to recover that cost from the customer, even if it ends its contract. Each state regulator would have to consider the standard and decide.

Both clocks start on a day that hasn't happened.

It also counts backward.

A state skips both clocks if, before enactment, it had put a comparable standard in place, held a proceeding on one, or its legislature had voted on one. Has Alaska done any of the three?

Alaska's Senate passed SB 250, 14 to 5. A House panel held it.

It passed May 16th and was heard and held in House Community and Regional Affairs two days later. Does one chamber's vote count as "the State legislature has voted"?

Every date on the record, and the one not set.

Three yeas. Three short. No start date.

Save this. If the date is ever set, both clocks run from it.

items.title: Right for Most of Alaska. Wrong for Kodiak.
items.summary: From Shelikof Strait the camera drops to Bull Lake and the trooper's AI search, pulls back to five bird zones, then sinks to the mud where the $150 lands.
items.content_html:
A Kodiak court file holds an AI answer's September 1st, the law's October 8th and a September 5th snipe hunt.

Right for most of Alaska. Wrong for Kodiak.

On September 5th, a Kodiak hunter took three snipe.

She had searched "Snipe season" on her phone. She told a trooper that, according to Google, the season began September 1st. Kodiak's zone opens October 8th.

The zone was in the parentheses.

"ADF&G sets the Wilson's Snipe hunting season in Alaska generally from September 1st through December 16th (or matching general migratory bird/waterfowl windows depending on the specific zone...)"

Five zones. Two opening days.

Southeast, Gulf Coast and Northern open September 1st. Kodiak and the Pribilof and Aleutian zone open October 8th. Unimak Island goes with the Gulf Coast.

Same length. Only the start moves.

She called troopers on herself the same afternoon.

No contest. A $150 fine.

The charge was a Class A misdemeanor. She pleaded no contest and was fined $150, the Alaska Beacon reported.

"I expect we'll see more of this type of thing in the future."

Spokesman Austin McDaniel says it's the first time he thinks the department has seen AI cited, and it doesn't track these cases. Google's own help page says AI Overviews "can and will make mistakes."

Read the zone before the date.

DPS says the one source of truth for hunts is ADF&G's regulations and emergency orders.

items.title: A Say on 5 Megawatts at Eielson, Until September 30th
items.summary: A wetland map and five spots offered to developers. Reactor, coal plant and data center sized in 5 megawatt blocks. Murkowski and two utilities on power, then the comment address.
items.content_html:
You have until September 30th to comment on site work for a 5 megawatt microreactor near wetlands at Eielson Air Force Base.

The public gets a say on 5 megawatts at Eielson.

A reactor site, east of the runway's south end.

The Air Force wants public input on work at the preferred site for a 5 megawatt Oklo microreactor, near Spruce Lake. It sits near wetlands, so federal law requires the ask first.

Clear it, dig it, fill it, level it.

That is the preconstruction work Air Force officials describe. Their wetland delineation for a draft Environmental Assessment finished in July. KUAC reports the draft is expected late next year.

Oklo would own it. The Air Force would buy the power.

It would supply the base electricity and heat. A 30-year fixed-price contract could follow a Nuclear Regulatory Commission license. Officials hope for 2030, if only an assessment is needed.

Same base. A second process.

Five spots near Eielson, offered to developers.

The Air Force solicitation covered land at JBER, Eielson and Clear, about 4,700 acres in all. Proposals were due June 29th. KUAC reported no project awarded as of mid-September.

5 megawatts, against a 100 megawatt bar.

Separate processes, shown for scale. Nothing in the record says the reactor would serve a data center.

"we are not able to support them because of an insecure energy base at this time"

Chugach Electric and Golden Valley Electric told ADN in May that they can't produce enough electricity for large data centers as Cook Inlet gas dwindles.

Comment by September 30th.

items.title: A Bigger Tank, Not a Bigger Engine. Bradley Lake and 2030
items.summary: On a relief map and a cutaway, a proposed 4.6-mile tunnel carries Dixon Glacier water to Bradley Lake for more energy, not more megawatts, ending on a 1991 to 2032 calendar that splits what exists from what is only filed.
items.content_html:
Fairbanks is burning 250,000 gallons of diesel a day, AEA's Curtis Thayer says.

About 38 percent more electricity. Its dam is slated for 2030.

A bigger tank, not a bigger engine.

A new diversion dam would send Dixon Glacier meltwater through a 4.6-mile tunnel into Bradley Lake and raise its pool about 16 feet. Capacity barely moves. The plant gets more water to spend.

4.6 miles of tunnel to carry glacier water.

AEA estimates the cost at about $400 million and expects construction to start in 2027 if federal approvals come through. FERC has the application under project P-8221-124.

It buys energy, not megawatts.

Today, Dixon's meltwater runs down the Martin River.

"There's nothing for tomorrow. There's nothing for next year."

Natural gas fuels about 80 percent of Southcentral's power generation, per KTUU. Fairbanks is burning 250,000 gallons of diesel a day, Thayer said. "They never did that last year."

The AI pitch runs on the same calendar.

The Air Force offered twelve parcels, about 4,700 acres, at JBER, Clear and Eielson for AI data centers. Its solicitation said the JBER sites had insufficient power and needed a new Chugach connection.

What exists, and what is only filed.

Until the glacier water arrives, should Railbelt AI data centers bring their own power?

items.title: Who Read It? The Labels on 90 Alaska News Articles
items.summary: A counter of 1,258 recorded meetings is set against one Axon police-data story that ran with no editor review on record.
items.content_html:
Alaska News says its old footer told every reader an article was "reviewed by editors," whether or not it was.

"Source access is not the same thing as editorial judgment."

90 articles in 48 hours. One human name on the review line.

Alaska News says every article carries a line saying whether a person reviewed it. Every human name on those lines was the editor-in-chief's, Cale Green.

The machine already does the reading.

Alaska News says its tool has sat through 1,258 recorded public meetings and 3,092 hours of audio. A team of five based in Anchorage runs it. How would a reader know who read each draft?

The right invention is the label.

When an editor has read the whole piece, the article says reviewed by, with a name. When no one has, it says that instead. Its old footer told every reader "reviewed by editors," regardless.

What the labels on 90 articles said.

Counted from the alaskanews.com news sitemap, September 26th. A label describes process, not accuracy, and can change after a later review.

Plenty of reading. One name on the record.

The risk it names itself.

Alaska News says some articles publish without a person reading them first. Its story on the Anchorage Assembly's Axon police-data memo ran as "AI-assisted. No editor review is on record for this article." That doesn't make it wrong. It tells you to check.

"The strongest protection is not my assurance. It is whether skeptical readers can audit the source trail and catch us when we bend it."

Alaska News says the source wins when a summary and its record disagree. Readers can only audit what the label tells them.

Should every AI-drafted story in Alaska say who reviewed it, by name?

items.title: Six Data Center Sites. Two Answer to Juneau.
items.summary: The maps ink the two state sites in gold and ring the four federal ones in dashes. All four candidates are quoted at equal size.
items.content_html:
From the North Slope to Cook Inlet, six sites could host data centers, and Alaska's next governor could reach two.

A disclosure. This deck was produced by an automated studio running on Claude, a model made by Anthropic. The Alaska Beacon reports that Kreiss-Tomkins' campaign has received large donations from people employed by Anthropic. The deck leaves that report out and quotes all four candidates at equal size, in alphabetical order, so no candidate is framed by it.

Six sites in play for data centers. Two answer to Juneau.

Two sit on state land. Four are federal calls.

The North Slope lease and the Houston land are decided in the Department of Natural Resources, whose commissioner the governor appointed. The Air Force decides three bases. FERC decides Cook Inlet's preliminary permit.

What they say about data centers.

"I'm a big believer in data centers." He said the groups he is talking to would produce their own power (Bronson, Republican, Commonwealth North forum). "I support a moratorium on data center development in Alaska until the Legislature can pass a comprehensive regulatory framework for that development in Alaska." (Kreiss-Tomkins, Democrat, September 8th forum). "I think we need to embrace it." Any data center, he said, must "bring their own energy." (Taylor, Republican, September 8th forum). "I will never allow Alaska to be littered with hyperscale data centers that take our resources and spoil our lands." (Wilson, Republican, by text message). Order is alphabetical by surname, not a ranking. Quotes as reported by the Alaska Beacon.

Milepost 390. State land, 50 years.

DNR proposes a 50-year lease on 715.4 acres beside the Dalton Highway, 26 miles south of Deadhorse. Its final decision would be signed by the Division of Oil and Gas, under authority delegated from the DNR commissioner. The same decision says what powers it.

"not interconnected to the Railbelt or any other Alaska utility grid"

A gas plant designed for 1 to 3 GW, all used on site. Two candidates raised the same point.

One state decision, three federal ones.

DNR proposes giving AIDEA about 19,950 acres two miles north of Houston. No final decision appears on the notice. The Air Force offered to lease about 4,700 acres at JBER, Eielson and Clear, with no award yet.

Filings close the day before the vote.

DeepGreen proposes a 100 MW subsea data center in Cook Inlet, and FERC decides its preliminary permit. The Kenai Peninsula Borough filed to intervene. The deadline is November 2nd.

Who signs each one.

Preliminary decision. No final decision on the notice, for the North Slope lease (ADL 422741), which DNR signs under the commissioner's delegation. For a data center bill, the Legislature, then the governor. Senate passed it 14 to 5, per the Beacon. The House didn't. A veto takes two-thirds to override. For JBER, Eielson and Clear, the Department of the Air Force. Proposals closed June 29th. No award. For the Houston land to AIDEA, DNR. No final decision on the notice. For Cook Inlet (P-15423-000), FERC, on a preliminary permit. Filings close November 2nd.

Save this. Check it again after November 3rd.

items.title: Tested at Nenana. Awarded in New York. Next stop unnamed.
items.summary: Aerial views over Nenana show the awards, the test area at true size, a scorecard against the clock and a season in test areas.
items.content_html:
In June, controlled fires were set along the Nenana-Totchaket Road, and machines from Nenana's airport had 8 hours to find them alone.

Tested at Nenana.

Anduril first. Dryad second. AURA third.

XPRIZE paid $4.55 million across both tracks. The autonomous track was decided in the Alaska finals, and Lockheed Martin's $1 million detection bonus also went to Anduril.

The exam was flown from Nenana's airport

For two weeks in June the finalists flew from Nenana Municipal Airport. UAF's drone center, ACUASI, managed the airspace. The test site lay along the Nenana-Totchaket Road corridor.

One fire. Ten minutes. 1,000 square kilometers.

Each team's machines watched alone for 8 hours. The goal was to detect and fully suppress a high-risk fire within 10 minutes of ignition.

One 10 minute gate is on the record, for detection

XPRIZE says AURA met the 10 minute detection gate. Dryad says it detected and verified the fire in 12 minutes or less. XPRIZE's release doesn't say any team fully suppressed a fire inside 10 minutes.

"The final prize remains on the horizon"

Adam Broecker, Lockheed Martin, September 23rd.

Alaska's 2025 fires covered nearly seven test areas

XPRIZE estimates Alaska's 2025 season burned 1.68 million acres. That is about 6,800 square kilometers, the 1,000 km² test area nearly seven times over. The tiles show area only, not where anything burned.

What comes next names no Alaska address

XPRIZE now moves to a 12 to 15 month Impact Phase to turn these systems into deployable tools. Dryad plans pilots in 2027 and names no location. The only Alaska institutions in the record are UAF and ACUASI.

Alaska hosted the exam. Should it get a seat in the Impact Phase?

items.title: What Mat-Su's Plate Reader Ban Actually Reaches
items.summary: The ordinance and its information memorandum carry six of the nine frames. The borough's own law enforcement page carries two. The Anchorage Daily News carries one.
items.content_html:
Five agencies police the Matanuska-Susitna Borough. The borough is not one of them.

Mat-Su banned plate readers the night it was heard.

ADOPTED UNANIMOUSLY. IN FORCE ON ADOPTION.

The borough wrote down what the machine is.

The chapter defines it as one or more high-speed camera units, alone or combined with algorithms and optical character recognition, turning images of plates, makes, models, colors and unique vehicle identifiers into computer-readable data.

The subject never changes.

66 data center pods. 330 to 350 turbines. 3.5 miles of cable. The federal notice never says how much seabed.

So far, the Cook Inlet data center is a document.

Applied.

DeepGreen Cook Inlet SPV, LLC filed an application for a preliminary permit on February 11th and supplemented it on June 26th. FERC signed the notice September 1st. The Federal Register published it September 4th.

Proposed.

66 modular subsea-compute hives, which the notice also calls data center pods. 330 to 350 marine hydrokinetic turbines. A 3.5 mile, 115 kV hybrid power and fiber-optic armored cable, landing in the Nikiski Industrial Corridor.

Priority.

"The sole purpose of a preliminary permit, if issued, is to grant the permit holder priority to file a license application during the permit term." It would not authorize construction, land-disturbing work or entry onto property owned by others.

100 megawatts

"The estimated annual generation of the DeepGreen Project would be 100 megawatts, which would primarily be utilized to power the subsea data center." A megawatt measures power, not a year of it. That is the notice's own wording.

What it says. What it doesn't.

IN THE FEDERAL NOTICE

Nobody called.

"We're going to file to intervene and oppose it, just so we have a position. We've had no communication with them." Anyone. Including a rival.

items.title: Every Notice Went Up
items.summary: The ten items as the ordinance writes them, what the state found, and the blank in the form.
items.content_html:
Who has to be told before somebody changes the weather over the southern Kenai? The answer is not the borough underneath.

EVERY NOTICE WENT UP. NONE CAME DOWN.

19 FLARES OVER THE SOUTHERN KENAI, AUGUST 23RD

Notice was given. It went up.

Federal law bars anyone from changing the weather without filing a report, and the rule sets that filing at least 10 days before the activity begins. Rainmaker asked Alaska DNR first, and it answered with a letter of no objection.

The drones flew over state land.

Because the flight was over state and not borough land, no borough permission was needed. The borough's own attorney put the limit in writing, that a second class borough has no authority to fully regulate this or the airspace.

19 million gallons is a hundredth of an inch.

Rainmaker flew 10 drone flights on August 23rd and its report puts the result at about 57 acre-feet, or roughly 19 million gallons, which works out to about 0.01 inches across the area. The state calls these modeled estimates, not water measured at the ground.

The borough's port was never drilled.

Rainmaker's press release was the first notice the borough had that drones carrying weather modification payloads were operating inside it. The flight was over state land, so no borough permission was needed.

The borough wrote a form.

Ten required items, on borough land only.

Ten questions. None about the model.

The state's own letter says the company uses drones, atmospheric observations, weather radar and modeling to identify clouds and conditions suitable for seeding. Every one of the ten items asks about the payload, the pyrotechnics or the flight.

Everyone can ask. Almost nobody can act.

Alaska has no framework specific to weather modification and no state permit is required for cloud seeding. This session carries 856 bills and not one of them is on the subject. Federal law takes a filing, not a permission.

One room. October 20th.

The public hearing on the ordinance is October 20th, and if the Assembly enacts it, it takes effect immediately. Until then it is introduced and not law.

items.title: Utqiagvik Observers and an Arctic Ocean Model
items.summary: The deck holds a season disc broken open where the records disagree, the observer's October 1st, 2019 entry, and ten author slots.
items.content_html:
Validation is what science does to data to decide if it is good enough. A paper published September 18th inverts that.

"Everyone is waiting for snow."

The model had already frozen the sea.

In 2019 the model froze the sea early. The coast froze late.

The paper publishes the direction and no magnitude. This drawing does the same. The two marks sit inside a declared break, so the space between them carries no value.

"It has rained so much that the roads are falling apart and we may have broken a temperature record. Everyone is waiting for snow. The bowhead whales are not close to Barrow yet either."

Over 12,000 observations, more than 1,500 km of coast.

Observers document sea ice, ocean conditions, weather, fish and marine wildlife, and unusual or extreme events. The program and the one before it have run since 2006.

which made hunting especially difficult.

Observers reported late freeze-up, warm conditions and stormy weather

The fall hunt took one whale.

Historical fall harvests have reached up to about 30. Spring is a separate season and is not in this count.

Most of the time the two records agree.

The paper reports the model generally captured the timing of seasonal changes, especially the end of the open water season. That is what makes one wrong season worth finding.

Ten authors. The observers are among them.

The paper says Indigenous observers are co-authors and shape its research questions, the interpretation of results and the priorities for model development. It argues Indigenous Knowledge can identify model deficiencies that conventional metrics miss.

A model can be broadly right and still wrong about the season you live in.

items.title: Out of Nenana and Back, With the Finding Pending
items.summary: The deck holds the paired samples, the hangar laboratory at the same airport, and five logged channels as empty rows.
items.content_html:
A 1,000 kilometre blood flight out of Nenana is documented down to five logged sensor channels. The finding is not published.

1,000 km of blood. Out of Nenana. Back to Nenana.

8 h 47 min aloft. Back at Nenana.

ACUASI, part of the University of Alaska Fairbanks, flew human blood for the International Testing Agency. UAF puts the flight at 8 hours and 47 minutes. The ITA's own release says only several hours.

Two samples each. One flew. One stayed.

The Interior Region EMS Council drew the blood at UAF the day before. It was anonymised and chilled, then split into two groups.

A 31 foot span, and a 200 pound bay.

They are twin engine aircraft with three cargo drop doors, and they work off dirt, grass, ice or tarmac. UAF is one of nine FAA designated test sites for uncrewed aircraft.

A circle tests the cargo. A line delivers the care.

The flight began and ended at Nenana Municipal Airport. Closing a route holds everything still except the blood, which is how you find out whether the blood minds. It also means this test measured a sample and not a delivery.

The distance was the point. Alaska had the distance.

"I'm not saying we're ready today, but I think we'll be ready tomorrow."

The laboratory was in a building at the same airport.

Sysmex equipped a satellite laboratory inside an airport hangar with XN-Series analysers. Dr. Sven Voss, who directs the WADA accredited laboratory in Dresden, ran it. Both groups were analysed on site.

Alaska supplied the distance.

Cathy Cahill, who directs ACUASI, describes nurses taking samples in a community and getting the medication back before they leave. That is a line, not a loop.

items.title: Update. The Plan Got 250,000. The Aircraft Got More
items.summary: Both award rows are drawn as freight on one aircraft floor, with the ten rows out of 217 that name a machine.
items.content_html:
Alaska's rural health program awarded $250,000 for a drone plan on August 14th. On September 4th it awarded $4,171,115 for aircraft.

THE AWARD SAYS IMPLEMENTATION NOT PLANNING

Ryan Air was awarded $4,171,115 to deploy "autonomous cargo drones and electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft" carrying pharmaceuticals and moving patients across roadless communities. IA means aircraft, not a study.

A FAMILY FREIGHT LINE WITH A GRANT

Ryan Air started in 1953 in the village of Unalakleet and is managed by the third generation of the Ryan family. It serves 80 villages throughout Western Alaska and operates 24 aircraft out of eight hubs.

AIRCRAFT TAKE THE PLACE OF AMBULANCES

402 Alaskan communities depend on aviation for year round access, where aircraft often take the place of cars, school buses, semitrucks, and ambulances. That is 82 percent of the state's communities, served by 235 airports. Ryan Air's own proposal calls the gap "life-threatening".

ONE PROGRAM. TWO LOADS.

THE INTERIOR GOT A YEAR TO PLAN

Tanana Chiefs Conference took $250,000 for a planning year on the same idea, a drone pharmaceutical route from a Fairbanks hub to 42 Interior villages across 94,000 square miles. Tanana Chiefs says winter medication delays of 5 to 14 days are common.

FIRST THE WAIVER THEN THE AIRCRAFT

Tanana Chiefs names the University of Alaska Fairbanks Alaska Center for Unmanned Aircraft Systems Integration as its partner on FAA beyond visual line of sight waivers. ACUASI was selected as one of the first seven FAA unmanned aircraft test sites.

TEN ROWS NAME A MACHINE

THE ROUNDS ARE NOT FINISHED

Roughly $65 million is still expected to be awarded ahead of a federal deadline of October 30th. The next Friday is the next row.

Two numbers and one blank sit in the stock table of the Arctic permit NMFS issued the Navy on September 10th.

The permit can find the robot. It can't count the seal.

Sound is how the machine knows where it is.

items.title: Section 1200 Is Called Interruption
items.summary: A 36 cell grid of the daily readings with the 2 unverified days left empty, and the tariff volume drawn end on with only its top step marked.
items.content_html:
Enstar, the gas utility for almost half of Alaska's population, publishes a tariff section numbered 1200 and titled Interruption.

Cook Inlet storage read 7,648,351 Mcf on September 10th. Design volume is not what the field can deliver on any given day.

Enstar sells gas to almost half of Alaska's population and gets nearly all of its supply from Hilcorp. Southcentral runs more than 70 percent of its electricity on gas, per Alaska Public Media citing ISER.

Enstar president John Sims told state lawmakers in August the utility was about 3 Bcf short of ideal storage.

A failed day carries no number forward. Demand model 2.0 is published in full. Its demand is modeled, not measured.

It is published on Enstar's own tariff page. Enstar says reductions would be phased by customer class under the tariff. The divisions below the top one are not drawn here.

Kenai Mayor Henry Knackstedt met Enstar's president and other Southcentral mayors on August 21st, then told his city council what Enstar described.

items.title: One Agenda. Two Items. One Vote.
items.summary: The carousel plots the network's real size on a log rule. 11 cameras integrated against 238 registered as of August 27th, 2026, under a 750 ceiling.
items.content_html:
A hearing on Anchorage's police AI rule was set for September 1st, 2026. The camera money passed 8 to 4 that night. The rule got no vote.

UPDATE. $598,998 passed 8 to 4. The rule got no vote.

Three of the four no votes wrote the rule.

Keith McCormick, Daniel Volland and Sydney Scout proposed AO 2026-108. All three voted against the money. They lost 8 to 4 on the night of September 1st, 2026.

What the money is, and what it is not.

The $598,998 comes from federal asset forfeitures, per a memorandum submitted to the Assembly. Chief Sean Case says it moves the crime center to its final location. The Assembly approved $11.8 million last year for the underlying system. ADN reported the Assembly considered a $600,000 ThunderCat contract.

750 is the ceiling, not the count.

The gap from 11 to 238 is wider than the gap from 238 to 750. Registered means APD knows the camera exists. Integrated means APD can pull the feed, through a CORE device from Axon.

Three gates. None of them struck.

ADN reports the ordinance would require Assembly permission before AI with human feature recognition is added to the network. Alaska Public Media reports it would require a warrant before data goes to federal agencies. ADN reports the technology would face a period of temporary approval and annual reporting.

CODE.

"Let's put this into code now, so that when power changes, when the political winds shift, as they always do, we have protections for the people, no matter who is overseeing and implementing the system."

What is already in code. And what is only practice.

Municipal use of facial recognition technology was officially banned by the Anchorage Assembly in 2023, per APD's own page. All scanned license plate data is automatically deleted after 14 days. Traffic camera footage is overwritten every 3 to 5 days. The camera registry is voluntary, the owner keeps control at all times, and APD must obtain permission to access video. APD does not use Flock cameras.

Fourteen days, read twice.

How long a scanned plate lives. Deleted after 14 days, per APD's own page. How long the rule waited. September 1st, 2026 to September 15th, 2026.

The rule is expected back on September 15th, 2026.

Sponsors plan to bring AO 2026-108 back to the Assembly. Public testimony is how a resident gets read into the record.

items.title: Run Both Instruments, or Lose the Record
items.summary: Slide 06 draws the survey gear's seabed footprint at true area, and slide 08 sets the three pools on one rail where the third bracket is empty.
items.content_html:
When a machine takes a ship's place on a fish survey, how do you tell a change in the fish from a change in the instrument?

Two instruments on the same line, in parallel. That's the bill.

The new instrument is allowed to be different.

"Consistency in information that FIS data products provide is more important than consistency in FIS methods."

Agreement is bought. It is never assumed.

The framework calls for "incremental incorporation and calibration of new technologies" rather than "a wholesale replacement of existing methods that would disrupt the historical baseline of a time series" (C05). The most common way to do it is to run the old method and the new one in parallel for a fixed period (C07).

Ground the net can't cross.

The camera can see it. It can't hold it.

NOAA says the camera techniques "are not intended to replace hands-on sampling because physical specimens are essential for critical data, including age, feeding habits, and body condition" (C20). A near-infrared machine reads an otolith in 30 to 50 seconds, more than 10 times faster than a human at a microscope (C18).

0.006%

The framework's own figure for the share of total Alaska seabed area that bottom trawl survey gear contacts, offered against calls to ban extractive sampling (C08).

The record is being pulled from two sides at once.

The framework lists funding, vessel availability, new sampling objectives and new technology as human forces that break a time series (C09). NOAA says fish populations have shifted into deeper water or farther north where surveys have not traditionally been conducted (C12).

Twelve days later, the same question, on a smaller boat.

On September 15th, 2026 the North Pacific Council's Partial Coverage Fishery Monitoring Advisory Committee reviews the draft 2027 Annual Deployment Plan (C22, C23). The 2026 plan defines a no selection pool, vessels with no probability of carrying an observer or an electronic monitoring system on any trip that season (C28).

The committee takes comment letters.

The draft 2027 Annual Deployment Plan had not yet been posted on the meeting page as of September 6th, 2026 (C25). The Federal Register notice says public comment letters will be accepted and should be submitted electronically through the meeting page (C24).

items.title: One Race Late. The limit and the money it missed.
items.summary: One sheet holds every gift in the 2026 record, photographed nine times, down to the inside of a single deposit.
items.content_html:
105 top Alaska donors match what six Bay Area donors gave governor candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins.

A disclosure. This deck was produced by an automated studio running on Claude, a model made by Anthropic, and it reports on donations by six people who list Anthropic as their employer. The company gave nothing and no company statement about the donations is reported. Every figure here is arithmetic over the State of Alaska's own disclosure rows, recomputed twice by separate code, and an adversarial fact-check dropped twelve claims before publication.

It takes 105 Alaska donors to match six people Outside.

Six gifts. $372,000. Every one from the Bay Area.

At this distance the median Alaska gift is a whole gift.

Alaska sent most of the gifts. Not most of the money.

86 donors carried 72.81 percent of it.

117,962 to 45,418.

The same ink, twice.

The money went to the candidate who wants data centers stopped.

Four tickets. Old rules.
